analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workers' rights to form unions and collectively bargain.
analysis.headline: The bill had 219 cosponsors — every House Democrat and 3 Republicans — but was referred to committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill, named for the late union president Richard Trumka, overhauls the main federal law covering union organizing. It widens who counts as an employee covered by labor law, lets unions win bargaining rights with fewer employer delays, bans permanent replacement of striking workers, allows secondary strikes, overrides state laws barring mandatory union fees, makes it an unfair labor practice to force workers to attend anti-union meetings or sign away their right to join class-action lawsuits, adds whistleblower protections, and raises penalties on employers who break the rules — up to $50,000 per violation, doubled for repeat offenders. It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and died there without any action.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to form unions, union members, and employees facing employer tactics like captive anti-union meetings, permanent striker replacement, and forced arbitration agreements. Union membership is historically associated with higher wages and benefits, so the bill's core beneficiaries are employees seeking to organize or bargain collectively.

how_it_helps.text: Widens coverage under labor law: adopts a multi-factor test limiting who can be classified as an independent contractor and makes companies that share control over workers' terms of employment joint employers, so workers can bargain with the companies that actually set their conditions.

Bans employers from permanently replacing or discriminating against workers who strike, and makes it an unfair labor practice to require or coerce employees to attend employer meetings designed to discourage union membership.

Speeds up union elections with tighter timelines, allows remote voting by phone or internet, removes employer standing to intervene in representation proceedings, and lets the Board certify unions as bargaining representatives when an employer's misconduct tainted an election.

Raises the stakes for breaking labor law: civil penalties up to $50,000 per violation (doubled to $100,000 for repeat violators), personal liability for directors and officers, liquidated and punitive damages for fired workers, and the right to go directly to court.

Prohibits forced arbitration agreements under which workers waive the right to pursue or join class or collective litigation over employment disputes, and adds whistleblower protections including reinstatement and back pay.

analysis.who_pays: Employers — especially large employers, franchisors, staffing firms, and gig-economy platforms that rely on classifying workers as independent contractors — would face higher compliance costs, expanded liability, penalties, and a greater likelihood of unionization. In right-to-work states, employees in unionized units could be required to pay representation fees despite state law.

drawbacks.text: Section 111 would override state right-to-work laws, allowing collective bargaining agreements to require all employees in a unit to pay union fees as a condition of employment — a change critics describe as compelling financial support for unions over individual choice.

The bill permits secondary strikes — unions encouraging members to strike in sympathy with workers represented by a different union — and bars employers from suing over them, which opponents argue exposes bystander businesses to pressure campaigns.

It imposes binding arbitration for first contracts: if bargaining stalls after mediation, a tripartite panel sets terms binding for two years, with criteria including workers' ability to sustain themselves and wages at comparable employers — a shift that critics say takes contract terms out of the hands of the parties.

The independent-contractor test could reclassify many freelancers and gig workers as employees, which would give them organizing rights and benefits but could also cost them the flexibility of contractor status and create compliance burdens for the businesses that engage them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the upside is substantial: faster elections, real penalties for firing organizers, an end to permanent striker replacement, and protection against forced arbitration. The costs fall on employers, and some provisions are genuinely contestable — overriding state right-to-work laws, permitting secondary strikes, and mandatory arbitration of first contracts all draw principled objections beyond pure business self-interest, and the contractor reclassification has real tradeoffs for workers who prefer independence. On balance, the bill is a broad transfer of bargaining power to employees and unions at employers' expense.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced in February 2023, never got a hearing or markup, and died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 28, 2023 by Rep. Bobby Scott and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
It attracted 219 cosponsors — all 216 House Democrats and 3 House Republicans.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action; the bill's last recorded action is the original committee referral.
The Congress ended January 3, 2025, so the bill expired without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and business groups that opposed the bill keep the current legal landscape: no new penalties, no secondary strikes, no override of right-to-work laws, and no change to how gig workers are classified. The bill's supporters gained nothing this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split almost perfectly by party: all 216 House Democrats signed on, versus 3 of 224 Republicans, and the committee that buried it was chaired by a Republican in a Republican-run House.

industries.industry: Large employers and unions' target workplaces
industries.note: The bill raises penalties to $50,000 per violation, makes officers personally liable, bans permanent striker replacement and captive anti-union meetings, and speeds up elections — all making unionization and worker litigation cheaper and easier for workers and costlier for employers. Its defeat preserved the status quo.

The new employee and joint-employer definitions would likely reclassify many contractors as employees and make companies that share control over workers jointly liable for bargaining — a direct threat to business models built on contractor status. Their interest runs against the workers seeking coverage.

Unions would gain faster elections, secondary strikes, fair-share fees notwithstanding state law, and binding arbitration for first contracts — tools that also strengthen workers' collective power, though fee requirements would apply to workers regardless of individual preference.
The joint-employer standard would hold companies accountable for workers controlled in fact by franchisees or agencies, ending the structural insulation from labor obligations.

The bill voids pre-dispute arbitration agreements requiring workers to give up class or collective employment claims, shrinking the market for mandatory employment arbitration and restoring workers' day in court.
